newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Ex-dissident back in Moscow as Israeli minister.
newsitem.headline: Ex-dissident back in Moscow as Israeli minister.

text.p: Natan Sharansky returned to Moscow as an honoured Israeli minister on Monday, 10 years after he was freed from a KGB jail and turned over to the West in one of the most dramatic Cold War prisoner swaps.

Sharansky, a Soviet-era dissident who served nine years on charges of spying for Washington, was received with diplomatic courtesies at Moscow's main airport and driven off in a flagged embassy car for ministerial talks -- a far cry from the barred prison van that took him on his last journey through Moscow.
His bearing was decidedly that of a politician and diplomat, a visiting trade and industry minister, rather than a former dissident and prison inmate.

"I am returning to a new country which enjoys freedom together with all of us...with which we can work together," Sharansky, huddled in a heavy black coat and Russian-style fur hat, told reporters on arriving.
"This also means the closing of some important circle in our lives. Where yesterday we had to struggle one against the other, today we can work together."
But clearly the visit had a bitter-sweet personal edge.

Sharansky, now 49, planned to visit the Lefortovo KGB prison in Moscow where he was held after his arrest in 1977, but he says he has been denied permission to go to the labour camp where he served most of his term.
"They are embarassed," he said before the visit. "I asked for the labour camp. They said no...You know, it has changed, but not to the end (completely)."

Sharansky, formerly Anatoly Shcharansky, was one of the most prominent political prisoners of the Soviet era. His campaigning for Jewish emigration rights was a bane to the KGB, but the espionage charges raised against him were regarded in the West as severe even by the standards of the time.

After almost 10 years in jail he was released on February 11, 1986, at the Glienicke Bridge linking West Berlin with Potsdam in East Germany in one of the last, and certainly the most public, prisoner swaps of the Cold War.

Sharansky crossed the iron bridge to West Berlin on an icy February day in the full glare of dozens of television cameras as a group of Soviet Bloc spies crossed in the other direction to East Germany.

Soon afterwards he changed his name to Natan and began a new life in Israel. He says he never felt any nostalgia for Russia and turned down an invitation to visit soon after the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union.
But he says he also harbours no bitterness.

"If I left defeated or humiliated, probably I would feel very vengeful, but the thing is that I always felt...that really it was a great victory and they lost. They were destroyed," he said before the visit.

Sharansky, his features somewhat heavier but largely unchanged from those of the man who crossed the bridge, was accompanied by his elderly mother Ida Milgrom, who had followed her son into exile. Both smiled and laughed as they were greeted by old friends and acquaintances at Sheremetyevo's VIP lounge.

Sharansky was scheduled to meet Moscow's reforming mayor Yuri Luzhkov later on Monday and Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Fortov. On Tuesday he was expected to visit the grave of Soviet dissident scientist Andrei Sakharov, who was forced into internal exile three years after Sharansky was jailed.
Sharansky was made a minister in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government after the success of his Yisrael ba-Aliya (Israel of Immigration) party in Israel's parliamentary elections last May.

He brought with him a group of 60 Israeli businessmen with the aim of boosting bilateral trade in his five-day visit. His talks with Russian officials will focus on agricultural technology, medical equipment and telecommunications.
Israeli officials say bilateral trade, virtually non-existent five years ago, is now worth about $500 million a year and expanding fast.
